prompt.context: The maker of Botox is considering expanding to the migraine market and has already begun clinical trials in this area. The product is expected to receive FDA approval in 2016. Your team has been hired to assess the viability of this product for launch.
prompt.question: How will you determine if the market is attractive? If the market is attractive, do you have any recommendations regarding how to launch the product? What concerns should the client take into consideration before deciding to launch? At the conclusion of the case you will need to present your team's recommendation and rationale.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of the product?
clarifying_info.a: The drug will be priced at $200 per injection.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs associated with the launch?
clarifying_info.a: Remaining development and launch costs amount to approximately $5B. Manufacturing marginal costs are expected to be quite small. Annual marketing expense can be estimated at $1B.

clarifying_info.q: How is the product administered and how often?
clarifying_info.a: It is a prophylactic injection given every 2 months.

clarifying_info.q: How does the product compare to existing treatments?
clarifying_info.a: It offers similar efficacy compared to the market-leading option but without any side effects. When taken for migraines it also has some added skin care benefits.
The market-leading branded prescription oral migraine treatment lost patent protection last year. There is a strong over-the-counter generic market for migraine treatments.

clarifying_info.q: What share of the market can Botox expect to capture?
clarifying_info.a: Due to the absence of side effects and the beneficial skin care properties, assume 20%–40% of the overall market in 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What share of migraine sufferers are willing to try this medicine?
clarifying_info.a: Assume at least 10% of migraine sufferers are willing to try such a medicine. (Alternatively, assume 50% of chronic migraine sufferers experience severe migraines and are willing to purchase prescription products.)

clarifying_info.q: Is this only for the US market?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, this drug will initially be produced in the US; use a US population of 300 million.

framework: 1. Market sizing: Estimate the size of the US prescription migraine market in patients and dollars
2. Revenue and profitability assessment: Compare projected revenue to development, launch, and ongoing marketing costs
3. Launch considerations: Evaluate branding, cannibalization, competition/formulary, regulatory, and patient-adoption risks
4. Recommendation: Synthesize findings into a go/no-go recommendation with key risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Estimate the size of the US prescription migraine market and Botox's potential annual revenue.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a top-down market size using US population, prevalence of chronic migraines, share of severe sufferers who use prescription drugs, price per injection, and injection frequency. Expected market share of 20%–40% should be applied to arrive at Botox-specific revenue. Strong candidates will also compare revenue to the $5B launch cost and $1B annual marketing spend to assess profitability.

math.setup: US population × % chronic migraine sufferers × % severe (prescription-willing) = total addressable patients. Multiply by annual revenue per patient to get total market $. Apply Botox market share to get Botox annual revenue.
steps: Price per injection: $200; injections per year: 12 months ÷ 2 months = 6
math.answer: Total US prescription migraine market ≈ $36B annually; Botox potential annual revenue ≈ $7B–$14B.

questions.prompt: What concerns should the client take into consideration before deciding to launch?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will cover at least four categories: (1) Branding — the Botox brand carries a cosmetic/controversial image that may reduce patient willingness and creates shared risk exposure if a new side effect is discovered in the larger migraine population; (2) Cannibalization/Erosion — launching at a lower price point than the cosmetic indication could drive off-label use, price erosion, and cannibalization of the existing cosmetic segment; (3) Competition/Formulary — similar efficacy to generics may prevent formulary inclusion, limiting reimbursement and patient access; (4) Regulatory — the FDA may require different labeling or restrict prescribing to certain specialties; (5) Patient adoption — patients are generally averse to injectable therapies when oral options are available. The interviewer should push the candidate to justify each concern.

brainstorming.prompt: What concerns should the client take into consideration before deciding to launch Botox for migraines?

categories.name: Branding
ideas: Botox brand carries a cosmetic and somewhat controversial image that may deter patients seeking a non-cosmetic treatment
Shared brand name creates risk: a newly discovered side effect in the large migraine population could damage the existing cosmetic franchise
Separate branding could reduce these risks but may sacrifice brand-recognition advantages

categories.name: Cannibalization and Price Erosion
ideas: Launching the migraine product at $200/injection vs. higher cosmetic pricing may encourage off-label cosmetic use at lower prices
Physicians and patients may identify the two products as identical, making it difficult to sustain separate markets
Regulatory and contractual mechanisms should be explored to keep the markets distinct

categories.name: Competition and Formulary Access
ideas: Similar efficacy to now-generic oral treatments weakens the value proposition for payers
Insurance companies may decline to add the product to formulary, leaving patients to pay out-of-pocket
A targeted indication (e.g., patients for whom oral treatments fail) could improve formulary negotiations

categories.name: Regulatory
ideas: FDA approval for a new indication of an existing product can require separate labeling and prescribing restrictions
Marketing may need to target specific specialties (neurology, headache clinics), increasing complexity and cost
International approvals could expand the addressable market but add regulatory burden

categories.name: Patient and Physician Adoption
ideas: Patients generally prefer oral treatments over injections; adoption may be slower than market share estimates suggest
A bi-monthly injection schedule requires ongoing physician visits, adding inconvenience vs. daily oral pills
Physician education and awareness programs will be needed to drive uptake

recommendation: The US prescription migraine market is large (~$36B) and Botox's projected annual revenue of $7B–$14B suggests strong profit potential even after the $5B launch cost and $1B annual marketing spend.

However, launching under the Botox brand name poses significant cannibalization and reputational risks. Launching under a separate brand name is recommended to allow independent pricing, differentiated advertising, and protection of the existing cosmetic franchise.
risks: Regulatory: FDA approval for the new indication is not yet secured; the entire business case depends on this.
Branding: Using the same name risks brand damage if adverse events occur in the larger migraine population; using a different name risks lack of market traction.
Cannibalization: A lower migraine price point could trigger substantial off-label use and price erosion in the cosmetic segment.
Formulary: Payers may refuse to reimburse without a differentiated efficacy claim versus generics, limiting patient access.
next_steps: Continue clinical trials and pursue FDA approval for the migraine indication.
Establish regulatory, brand, and marketing barriers between the cosmetic and migraine markets (e.g., distinct brand, separate sales force, specialty-restricted prescribing).
Negotiate contracts with major insurance companies and PBMs to secure formulary placement before launch.
Evaluate whether a specific patient subpopulation (e.g., treatment-resistant migraines) can be targeted to strengthen the value proposition and formulary case.
Assess potential for international regulatory submissions to expand the addressable market.
